newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Troops move into riot-torn Indonesian town.
newsitem.headline: Troops move into riot-torn Indonesian town.

text.p: Hundreds of Indonesian troops moved into a riot-torn town in western Java late on Thursday after a mob set fire to commercial buildings and churches, residents and military officials said.

"The situation is still tense. We hope we will get it under control," an officer who refused to be named told Reuters by phone from the battered town of Tasikmalaya, about 200 km southeast of Jakarta.
There were no immediate reports of casualties or arrests.

The mob estimated by police and residents at around 5,000 people, many of them youths, was apparently incensed by reports that police had beaten a religious teacher and his two students. "Yes, the rioting is connected to that case," a Tasikmalaya police official told Reuters.

The army officer said at around 9 p.m. (1400 GMT) that at least five battalions of troops -- more than 1,000 men -- had been sent to the town of some 500,000 people, a road and rail transit point on the way to central Java.

Residents contacted by phone said the crowd ran amok after reports of the police beatings. They said trouble had broken out in the morning when crowds started to gather outside police offices following rumours that one of the people allegedly beaten had died. There was no confirmation of this.
They said the town, also a centre of handicraft production, had suffered heavy damage, with department stores and shops on the main streets set afire. Police said three churches were also torched.

Soldiers used five trucks to ferry people out of the town centre to safety in army barracks, a resident said. He said the main streets were full of soldiers, but there were fears of further trouble in outlying areas.
Witnesses said police and troops cordoned off the town, which looked as if it was under siege.
In the last major riot in mainly-Moslem Indonesia, 25 churches and a temple were burnt down and five people died in October after a mob rampaged in the Situbondo area of East Java.
This riot was sparked by a court case in which a Moslem heretic subsequently received a jail term for blasphemy.
Political and religious analysts say Christian churches become targets for mob violence primarily for economic and social reasons, with Christians usually the more affluent members of the community.

Indonesia's Armed forces chief General Feisal Tanjung said in Irian Jaya province on Wednesday that conflicts triggered by religious differences were more dangerous than those caused by ethnic and racial differences, the official Antara news agency reported.
The trial of five Indonesians accused of taking part in the Situbondo riots opened on December 17. They were the first of 53 people expected to face trial.
More than 80 percent of Indonesia's nearly 200 million people are Moslems, but the government recognises all the world's major religions.
